one_liner: AVX-512IFMA X25519/Ed25519 code plus an OpenSSL 1.1.1 ENGINE; beats OpenSSL's x86-64 Curve25519 code 3.3-12x on throughput.
what_it_does: This is the artifact for the USENIX Security 2024 paper on ENG25519. It has two parts: X25519 and Ed25519 primitives written for AVX-512IFMA (Crypto/Curve25519_AVX512IFMA), and an OpenSSL ENGINE (ENG25519/eng25519) that plugs them into OpenSSL 1.1.1 through EVP_PKEY methods, so TLS applications such as openssl s_server and unbound use them after a config-file change, with no code changes. The raw primitives have their own API: x25519_batch_keygen_8x1w makes eight keypairs per call, ed25519_sign_1x8w signs one message, and ed25519_verify_1x2w verifies one signature. The ENGINE hides the batching behind a pool of pre-generated keypairs.
how_it_is_fast: Field elements mod 2^255-19 are stored in radix 2^51 (five limbs) to fit the 52-bit vpmadd52luq/vpmadd52huq multiply-add instructions, and field arithmetic runs 8x1-way: eight independent field elements across the eight 64-bit lanes of a zmm register. The paper's 'maximize transferable parallelism' idea carries that 8-way parallelism up the stack. KeyGen runs eight independent fixed-base scalar multiplications per call (8x1 -> 8x1 -> 8x1), Sign spreads one table-based fixed-base scalar multiplication over 8 lanes (8x1 -> 8x1 -> 1x8), and Verify uses a 2x4-way window-based double-point scalar multiplication (8x1 -> 2x4 -> 1x2, window width 5). The ENGINE's X25519-Derive is not the authors' code but a wrapper around Hisil et al.'s AVX-512F 4-way Montgomery ladder.
when_to_use: TLS 1.3 servers whose throughput is limited by handshakes, running OpenSSL 1.1.1 on Intel Xeons with AVX-512IFMA (Ice Lake or newer) and using X25519 key exchange with Ed25519 certificates. The paper measured 25% more handshakes per second than stock X25519 (1,707 vs 1,366) and 24-41% higher DoT peak throughput.
Bulk generation of ephemeral X25519 keypairs, where eight keypairs per call fits naturally (key pools, precomputed keypairs for session setup).
Services that sign a lot of Ed25519 on AVX-512IFMA servers: about 24.7k cycles per signature, versus 93.6k for OpenSSL 1.1.1's C code.
A reference design for AVX-512IFMA Curve25519 arithmetic, with CryptoLine-verified field routines, or for handling the cold start of AVX-512 units in latency-sensitive code.
when_not_to_use: CPUs without AVX-512IFMA, which includes AVX2-only parts, Cascade Lake and Cooper Lake Xeons (per the paper) and ARM. There is no fallback path, and the build uses -march=native.
OpenSSL 3.x or 4.x stacks. The ENGINE API was deprecated in OpenSSL 3.0, and OpenSSL 4.0.0 (April 2026) removed engine support, so ENG25519 would have to be ported to the provider API.
Workloads dominated by X25519 shared-secret derivation. The authors did not beat prior work there: the ENGINE's derive is Hisil et al.'s code at 61,867 cycles, only 1.47x OpenSSL 1.1.1.
Clients or lightly loaded servers. Cold AVX-512 units made the primitives 1.6-3.8x slower in the paper's DoT test, and the fix is a helper thread that keeps the vector unit awake.

Production code that needs maintained, audited crypto. This is a research artifact, stale since June 2024, with no releases. Only the field arithmetic is formally verified, and the authors never benchmarked it against Intel's own AVX-512IFMA multi-buffer crypto_mb Curve25519 code (issue #1).

integration.form: shared lib (OpenSSL 1.1.1 ENGINE loaded via openssl.cnf); the raw primitives are a source-drop with no library target (their CMake builds only a benchmark executable)
integration.dependencies: OpenSSL 1.1.1 (1.1.1q recommended; needed for SHA-512 and the ENGINE API), CMake 3.10+; the DoT experiments also use unbound
integration.min_toolchain: GCC 9.2.0 tested (C with inline AVX-512IFMA intrinsics plus GNU assembler files), built with -O2 -mavx512ifma -march=native
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux with AVX-512IFMA required (Intel Cannon Lake/Ice Lake or later, not Cascade/Cooper Lake); tested on Ubuntu (20.04 recommended for the DoT experiments)
integration.thread_safety: The ENGINE's keypair pool is protected by OpenSSL CRYPTO_RWLOCKs (one global lock and one per store). Thread safety of the raw primitives is not documented. One error path in batch.c (BATCH_CTX_new failing) returns while still holding the global lock.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — transparent for OpenSSL 1.1.1 applications once openssl.cnf loads the eng25519 ENGINE (X25519 and Ed25519 EVP_PKEY methods), but not usable with OpenSSL 3.x providers or OpenSSL 4.0, and the raw primitives have a different, batch-oriented API

gotchas: X25519 keygen through the ENGINE does not compute a fresh key per call. It hands out keys from a pool held in OpenSSL secure heap: 128 X25519 keypairs refilled by 16 batch calls, and 8 for Ed25519. Each refill stalls roughly 0.22-0.33 ms, according to the paper.
The ENGINE's X25519 derive never checks for an all-zero shared secret; its provider returns success unconditionally. The OpenSSL X25519() it replaces returns failure on an all-zero output.

The published speedups are warm-start numbers (2,000 warm-up runs). Cold-start cost in real TLS traffic is 1.6-3.8x higher unless you run the authors' timer_warmup or heuristic_warmup helper pinned to the sibling hyperthread, which also works against the CPU's power saving.

After the ENGINE's reference count drops to zero, the global lock is freed and never recreated, because the init is guarded by run_once. Re-initializing the ENGINE in the same process therefore fails.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you specifically need faster X25519/Ed25519 for TLS 1.3 on AVX-512IFMA servers. UltrafastSecp256k1 targets secp256k1 ECDSA (Bitcoin-style signing), fasthqc/hqc is a post-quantum code-based KEM, and VecFalcon (same first author) speeds up Falcon post-quantum signing, so none of them substitutes for Curve25519.
verified_claims_summary: Warm-start cycle counts were measured with GCC 9.2.0 -O2 on an Alibaba Cloud Xeon Platinum 8369B (Ice Lake, Turbo on), against OpenSSL 1.1.1's X25519 assembly and Ed25519 C code extracted into the same harness. The results: batched X25519-KeyGen 60,479 cycles per 8 keys vs 90,809 per key (12.01x throughput); Ed25519 sign 24,723 vs 93,606 cycles (3.79x) and verify 81,506 vs 271,445 (3.33x); fixed-base scalar multiplication 8.06x. Against Faz-Hernandez's AVX2 code the margins shrink to 1.18x for sign and 1.33x for verify, and end-to-end TLS 1.3 handshakes improved only 25%.
status_note: Stale research artifact (last commit June 2024, no releases, one open issue). It is LGPL-3.0, and the primitives are small enough to vendor, but the ENGINE is tied to an API that OpenSSL deprecated in 3.0 and removed in 4.0.
